\chapter{The Four Oldest Kinship Words}
\label{ch:sa-kinship}
\hlchaptermodality{23}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name a father, a mother, a son and a daughter in Sanskrit, and name a cousin of each outside India.}

Complete SA-C23-daughter and say all four words in order.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[pitā]{\sk{पिता} (pitā) — father}

\label{lesson:SA-C23-father}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{dahati} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{पिता}}
\textbf{\sk{पिता}} (\emph{pitā}) — \textquotedblleft{}father\textquotedblright{}.

The stem behind it is \textbf{\sk{पितृ}} (\emph{pitṛ-}), and its family reaches further than that of any word you have met: Latin \emph{pater}, Greek \emph{patēr}, Gothic \emph{fadar}, Old Irish \emph{athir}, English \emph{father}. The people lesson laid out four noun endings; this is a fifth family, the \emph{-ṛ} stems, and most of Sanskrit's kinship words live in it.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The first of the four oldest words in the family. Three follow, and each reuses the ones before.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{pitā}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item it beside \emph{pater} and \emph{father}, and hear the one word underneath
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \sk{पिता} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}father\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[mātā]{\sk{माता} (mātā) — mother}

\label{lesson:SA-C23-mother}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{pitā} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{माता}}
\textbf{\sk{माता}} (\emph{mātā}) — \textquotedblleft{}mother\textquotedblright{}.

The stem is \textbf{\sk{मातृ}} (\emph{mātṛ-}) — the same \emph{-ṛ} family as \sk{पिता}, and the same long reach: Latin \emph{māter}, Greek \emph{mētēr}, Old English \emph{mōdor}, English \emph{mother}, Russian \emph{mat}. Put the father-word into the dual and Sanskrit gives you \emph{pitarau}, 'the two parents', with the mother folded silently inside it.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Two of the four, and one ending family carrying both.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{mātā}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item it after \emph{pitā}, and name the ending they share
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \sk{माता} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}mother\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[sūnuḥ]{\sk{सूनुः} (sūnuḥ) — son}

\label{lesson:SA-C23-son}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{mātā} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{सूनुः}}
\textbf{\sk{सूनुः}} (\emph{sūnuḥ}) — \textquotedblleft{}son\textquotedblright{}.

From \textbf{√\sk{सू}} (\emph{sū}), 'to bring forth, to give birth' — so the word means the one who was brought forth. Its cousins are Gothic \emph{sunus}, Old English \emph{sunu}, English \emph{son}, Lithuanian \emph{sunus}, Russian \emph{syn}. Sanskrit's other son-word, \emph{putraḥ}, is far commoner in the texts and has no such relatives; this quieter one is the inherited word.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Three of the four, and a root that names a person by what happened to them.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{sūnuḥ}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item it beside \emph{sunus} and \emph{son}, and hear the one word underneath
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \sk{सूनुः} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}son\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[duhitā]{\sk{दुहिता} (duhitā) — daughter}

\label{lesson:SA-C23-daughter}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{sūnuḥ} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{दुहिता}}
\textbf{\sk{दुहिता}} (\emph{duhitā}) — \textquotedblleft{}daughter\textquotedblright{}.

Back to the \emph{-ṛ} family: the stem is \textbf{\sk{दुहितृ}} (\emph{duhitṛ-}), standing beside \sk{पिता} and \sk{माता}. Its cousins are English \emph{daughter}, Greek \emph{thugatēr}, Gothic \emph{dauhtar}, Persian \emph{duxtar}. Indian tradition read it as 'the one who milks', from \textbf{√\sk{दुह्}} (\emph{duh}) — a tidy story about a daughter's work in the house, which comparative linguists do not accept, because the cousins are older than the pun. Keep the story, and keep the fact that it is one.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
That closes the run: father, mother, son, daughter — the four words the family kept longest.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{duhitā}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item all four in order, and name the ending three of them share
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \sk{दुहिता} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}daughter\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
